name: Kriang-Khlor
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Gehrmann, Ryan (2017). The Historical Phonology of Kriang, A Katuic Language. JSEALS 10.1

new_statements.quote: The adverbial descriptive is the highest point of the clause or sentence intonation. Usually two syllables make up the descriptive. The syllable patterns are: CV(F) CV(F), or CV(C)CV(F). [...] In a reduplicated couplet the last syllable of the couplet receives the greatest stress of the word and has the highest intonation of the clause or sentence. The first word or syllable of the couplet is usually on a level tone like the rest of the clause or sentence; the last syllable receives greater stress, higher intonation and longer duration.
new_statements.citation: Smith, Ronald L. 1973. Reduplication in Ngeq. Mon-Khmer Studies 4: 85-111.
new_statements.locator: sec. 1.2 Intonation, p. 88 (PDF p. 4; page image redup_ocr/)
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Ngeq's two-syllable reduplicated descriptive couplets the last syllable carries the greatest stress of the word, together with the highest pitch and longest duration; the first syllable is level like the rest of the clause. This is consistent with the Katuic iambic word template (Gehrmann 2018: 133, main/final syllable always prominent, presyllable always unstressed; Kriang listed in Table 5) and with Chia 2014: 13 (pre-syllables 'typically unstressed'), so word stress falls on the final (main) syllable; no source gives a dedicated stress rule for ordinary non-reduplicated Ngeq words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Smith's statement is restricted to reduplicated adverbial-descriptive couplets and is framed as intonation; he adds (p. 104) that noun reduplications do not change sentence intonation. Chia 2014's 'typically unstressed' for pre-syllables is hedged and cited from Alves 2006 rather than argued for Ngeq.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (the 'stress of the word') for disyllabic descriptive couplets, but tied to clause/sentence intonation (the couplet is the intonation peak of the clause); the Katuic-general statements concern the maximally disyllabic prosodic word. No citation-form or instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the same language ngeq1245 [ngt]: Smith 1973 'Ngeq' (Se Kong river, Saravane province; treats Ngeq, Ngkriang and Khiang as dialects of one language); Chia 2014 'Ngeq (also known as Kriang)' with speakers from villages near Pakse, Champasak; Gehrmann 2017/2018 'Kriang' (Sekong province; dialects Kriang Kaleum and Kriang Tha Taeng). Smith's stress statement is about reduplicated descriptive couplets, not a general word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Gehrmann, Ryan. 2018. Katuic presyllables and derivational morphology in diachronic perspective. In H. Ring & F. Rau (eds.), Papers from ICAAL 7 (JSEALS Special Publication 3), 132-156. hdl:10524/52438
sources.note: p. 133: Katuic languages have 'prosodic words of a maximally disyllabic, iambic template'; Proto-Katuic word: 'The final syllable or main syllable of a disyllabic word is always prosodically prominent and phonotactically unrestricted while the penultimate syllable or presyllable is always unstressed'. Table 5 p. 136 lists Kriang under 'Marginal Presyllables'. Family-level statement; Kriang named but not separately described for stress.

sources.note: Sec. 2.1 Word and syllable structure, p. 13: words mono- or disyllabic, many disyllables sesquisyllabic (pre-syllable + main syllable); 'These pre-syllables are typically unstressed, have simple structures and typically include a reduced vowel nucleus (Alves 2006)' -- a Mon-Khmer generalisation with a citation, not a Ngeq-specific finding. No stress section; no stress marks anywhere in transcriptions, texts or the wordlist (pp. 75 ff.). Speakers from villages near Pakse (Champasak).
Nothing on stress; reference check only (cites Gehrmann 2017, Sidwell 2005, Sidwell 2021 classification chapter, Miller 2017 Katang kinship).
